provenance.setting: A prosperous wool-market town's square — the guild's hall and the merchant houses around it, raised in dressed limestone ashlar by masons to a polite classical order, not by carpenters in the vernacular. Money is spent on a formal frontage: pilastered bays, a round-arched ground arcade, worked quoins, and a shallow lead roof.

sources.dressed-limestone-ashlar: geology — limestone from the town quarry, squared and coursed by masons (abundant for a market town that can pay for the cutting) — typical use: wall fields, full height, in place of rubble and frame
sources.fine-coursed-ashlar: geology — finer, closer-jointed ashlar courses worked for the upper storey and the chimney shaft (common) — typical use: the storey above the arcade, stacks
sources.polished-freestone: geology — a pale freestone dressed and rubbed smooth for the pilaster order and string courses (costly, the frontage's pride) — typical use: the classical order articulating the bays
sources.worked-quoin-stone: wealth_class — crisply worked corner stones, arch voussoirs and a moulded chimney cap, cut by a mason where a clean classical edge must turn (scarce, spent on show) — typical use: quoins, voussoirs, cap
sources.imported-lead-and-slate: trade — lead and grey slate landed and carted in for a shallow prestige roof (imported) — typical use: the polite low-pitch roof a town frontage wears
sources.riven-stone-slate-courses: trade — stone-slate laid in graded courses up the shallow pitch (imported with the lead) — typical use: the coursed roof skin
sources.panelled-hardwood-joinery: timber — seasoned hardwood for a panelled town door, the one fine timber on a stone frontage (common) — typical use: the main door leaf
sources.crown-glass: trade — real crown-glass panes set in the windows, the mark of a town house over a cottage (imported) — typical use: glazed sash lights
sources.wrought-iron-work: trade — a little wrought iron landed for a door-lantern bracket and the area railings (scarce) — typical use: door lamp, railings to the area

provenance.wealthClass: Burgess wealth — a market town that can afford masons and a classical frontage: dressed ashlar throughout (not rubble-and-frame), a pilaster order, round-arched openings, and glazed crown-glass windows. The polite architectural language is the point; nothing is left in the vernacular.
provenance.roofingEconomy: A shallow lead-and-slate roof — the prestige low pitch a town frontage wears, laid in graded stone-slate courses. No steep timber gable: the roof is masonry's quiet partner, not a carpenter's pitch.

palette.rationale: The ground storey is full-height dressed limestone ashlar — squared and coursed by masons, the polite town wall that replaces the cottage's rubble-and-frame entirely. Pale worked stone at L65, it carries the arcade and reads as a built classical wall, not a vernacular field.

Crisply worked corner stones turn the classical edge the smooth field cannot — rusticated quoins a shade darker (L50) than the ashlar, the mason's hand where two faces meet. Spent on the corners and the chimney, the polite frontage's accent of worked stone.

The storey over the arcade is finer closer-jointed ashlar — coursed stone brick at L51, the same masonry carried full height with no plaster-on-timber upper. The wall is one material from plinth to cornice; the storeys are read by the pilaster order, not by a change of stuff.

The pilaster order articulating the bays is pale freestone dressed and rubbed smooth — L78, the lightest worked stone on the frontage, standing proud of the field to read as the classical member. This is the polite style's signature: an applied order, not a structural timber frame.

The shallow prestige roof is lead and grey slate, carted in costly and laid low — dark grey at L23, the polite town pitch that no steep timber gable answers. It sits as masonry's quiet partner over the dressed walls, the opposite of a warm carpentered roof.
The graded stone-slate courses stepped up the shallow pitch — the stair member of the roof family, riven stone laid in lapped courses, sharing the grey of the lead field.
The flat stone-slate course at eave and shallow break — the same graded slate laid level where the low pitch eases, the slab member of the roof family.

The round-arched openings are turned in worked voussoirs of dressed stone — the classical arcade head, a semicircle of coursed stone brick, in place of a flat timber lintel. The arch is the opening grammar of the polite style.
The one fine timber on a stone frontage: a panelled hardwood town door, seasoned and dark, set in a dressed-stone reveal under the arcade. Joinery, not the cottage's sawn board.
Real crown-glass panes glaze the sash lights — the mark of a town house over a cottage's lattice or shutter. Bought-in glass set in the dressed-stone openings.
The stack is carried up in the same fine coursed ashlar as the upper wall — dressed stone, not rubble, the polite frontage holding its material to the chimney head.
A moulded worked-stone cap crowns the stack where weather drives hardest — the same mason's hand as the quoins and voussoirs, a dressed weathering the coursed shaft cannot turn.
